native_result.query: At what Socioeconomic levels is the advantage in completion rates for Black students more pronounced?
native_result.HypoA: The advantage in BA degree completion rates for Black students becomes more pronounced at higher SES levels indicated by a positive interaction term SES*is_Black(coefficient:0.6271 (significant))
native_result.HypoB: No SES level shows a Black completion-rate advantage; the Black-vs-other BA gap is negative at every level. The disadvantage is most pronounced in the lower-middle SES band (2nd quintile, SES −0.59 to −0.24: 0.88% vs 3.62%, −2.74 pp; similarly the 4th quintile −2.64 pp), and essentially disappears at the highest SES levels (top quintile, SES > 0.54: 3.45% vs 3.54%, −0.10 pp, CI −2.47 to +2.78). The SES×Black logistic interaction is positive and significant (+0.627, p=0.012), i.e., the Black completion penalty shrinks with SES, reaching near-parity at the top of the SES distribution.
native_result.WorkflowB: Loaded nls_ses_processed.csv (8,773 rows, zero missingness). Binned continuous SES into equal-frequency quintiles (primary), quartiles and terciles (robustness). Within each bin compared BA completion rates of Black vs non-Black (pooled; secondary Black-vs-White and Black-vs-Hispanic), reporting absolute pp gaps with 2,000-replicate bootstrap CIs, Wilson CIs for rates, and Black/other ratios. Sex-stratified replication and logistic GLM (BA ~ SES + Black + SES×Black) as continuous checks. Ranking by |gap|: quintile bins 2 and 4 most pronounced, top bin near-parity; pattern robust across bin counts and sexes, with the Hispanic-only comparator the main divergence.
